The formula بسم الله الله أكبر is recommended by many."}, {"id": "5:4/q36/p2", "position": "It is recommended; a Muslim's catch remains lawful even if omitted deliberately without contempt.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī and some Mālikīs rely on the broader permission and a report that a believer slaughters in God's name whether uttered or not; Ashhab distinguishes ignorance from contempt."}, {"id": "5:4/q36/p3", "position": "One should say God's name at the meal, including when remembered late.", "reasons": "The Prophet's meal instructions, the Umayya b. Ṣubḥ's strength."}, {"id": "5:4/q36/p4", "position": "Verbal naming is indispensable even when omission was forgetful.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās prefers the spoken tongue over metaphorical heart remembrance; al-Shaʿbī, Ibn Sīrīn, Nāfiʿ and Abū Thawr hold the stricter omission view."}, {"id": "5:4/q36/p5", "position": "Inward remembrance suffices.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports this alternative and argues that verbal speech is the literal meaning."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q37", "question": "What does واتقوا الله require here?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning targets legal care or excessive hunting.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q37/p1", "position": "Observe all the food and hunting limits, especially training, owner-directed catch and invocation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabrisī and others apply the general command to the preceding rulings; al-Biqāʿī asks hunters to scrutinize fine distinctions."}, {"id": "5:4/q37/p2", "position": "Avoid excessive or recreational killing and keep worship in view.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī warns against cruelty and arrogance; al-Ālūsī notes hunting's distraction from prayer and purity, while the ʿUrfuṭa report permits hunting for livelihood."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q38", "question": "What does سريع الحساب mean?", "turns_on": "Whether swiftness describes knowledge, near Judgment, or prompt requital.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q38/p1", "position": "God knows and counts every deed and can reckon all creatures simultaneously without calculation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qushayrī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī and al-Biqāʿī emphasize complete knowledge and no distraction; 21:47 is cited."}, {"id": "5:4/q38/p2", "position": "The Day of Reckoning is near or its accounting begins soon.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī compares 2:202; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī report this temporal sense."}, {"id": "5:4/q38/p3", "position": "Reckoning or requital is swift in this life.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī understand prompt worldly punishment; al-Bursawī's inward reading describes immediate spiritual consequence."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q39", "question": "How does the verse connect with surrounding passages?", "turns_on": "How permission specifies prohibitions and expresses the sūra's themes.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q39/p1", "position": "It resumes and explains 5:3's food prohibitions, especially carrion and the slaughter exception.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuranyolu connect permitted game to forbidden carrion; some distinguish actual and anticipated questions. 5:94 concerns sanctuary game."}, {"id": "5:4/q39/p2", "position": "The food rule fits the sūra's themes of God's legislative authority, covenant and blessings.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī emphasizes God alone declares lawful and the naming command counters polytheist omission; Study Quran links the opening rulings to blessings and covenant, and comparison with Moses' final sermon."}, {"id": "5:4/q39/p3", "position": "Good food is a divine favor whose lawful enjoyment calls for gratitude.", "reasons": "Study Quran connects 5:4 with manna, Israelite food changes, Jesus' relief and Muhammad's permission, citing 2:57, 3:50, 3:93, 4:160, 7:32 and 16:114."}, {"id": "5:4/q39/p4", "position": "The verse's concise sequence of food and hunting rules exhibits Qurʾānic eloquence.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī cites its wisdom and composition as an example of inimitability alongside legal and theological passages."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q40", "question": "What inward lessons are drawn?", "turns_on": "How the verse is read as a lesson about faculties and intentions.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q40/p1", "position": "Trained faculties should acquire virtues for God, not their own appetites.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads good things as divine realities and true knowledge, hunting animals as senses and faculties, training as moral sciences, owner-directed holding as selfless intention, naming as inward orientation, and swift reckoning as immediate imprint on the soul."}, {"id": "5:4/q40/p2", "position": "A trained dog's surrender models the servant's complete dedication; lawful food preserves the heart.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says forbidden food hardens and alienates the heart while lawful food brightens it; good manners raise the lowly, and heedless eating is disapproved."}, {"id": "5:4/q40/p3", "position": "Spiritual goodness is whatever does not interrupt the path to God.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī contrasts ego-directed consumption, clothing, speech and thought with obligations purified by witnessing; his immediate reckoning yields intimacy or estrangement, and he cites a maxim and al-Sāʾib's couplet."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q41", "question": "What other legal or textual details are attached to this verse?", "turns_on": "How ancillary reports, manuscript details, and general examples are attached.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q41/p1", "position": "Knowledge gives the trained animal and knowledgeable person higher standing.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī quotes ʿAlī that one's value lies in what one knows; al-Kashshāf advises students to seek expert teachers even by long travel, a point repeated by later authors."}, {"id": "5:4/q41/p2", "position": "The passage permits hunting for livelihood and frames it as lawful support for dependents.", "reasons": "The ʿUrfuṭa report says earlier messengers hunted and earning for one's family is striving; al-Qurṭubī nonetheless forbids purposeless killing."}, {"id": "5:4/q41/p3", "position": "The sūra contains many distinctive legal obligations, including trained game.", "reasons": "Abū Maysara counts eighteen; al-Qurṭubī as reported by Ibn ʿĀshūr counts nineteen, with food, purity, theft and testimony among them."}, {"id": "5:4/q41/p4", "position": "The verse's hunting exception qualifies the carrion ban but sanctuary restrictions still govern sanctuary game.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī describes specification and reconciliation, citing game caught inside versus outside the sanctuary."}, {"id": "5:4/q41/p5", "position": "This verse was included in the Prophet's letter to ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm.", "reasons": "Ibn Shihāb reports the letter from the command to fulfill contracts through swift reckoning."}, {"id": "5:4/q41/p6", "position": "The word مما is written joined in the codex.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī lists this instance in his discussion of joined spellings; broader rasm principles govern regional readings and pauses. He notes joined wording for مما in 5:4, regional codex alignment, written rather than inferred omission at pauses, Hamza's eased pause, and assimilation in joined spellings."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q42", "question": "What broader discussions appear in the collected passages?", "turns_on": "Which collected passages are direct commentary and which are general excursuses.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q42/p1", "position": "General literary theory explains common poetic themes and analogies without treating them as theft.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī distinguishes common praise and demonstrations by lion or sea analogy from borrowing."}, {"id": "5:4/q42/p2", "position": "A prologue says this sūra can yield ten thousand questions and surveys refuge, sects and doctrine.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites the seventy-three-sect report as well known and reasons that understanding evils sought refuge from requires extensive knowledge."}, {"id": "5:4/q42/p3", "position": "An excursus analyzes verbal and mental speech and divine speech.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī distinguishes act and product, internal speech, and eternal divine speech, citing a report about inward thought and a sacred hadith."}, {"id": "5:4/q42/p4", "position": "The grammatical discussion of مِن compares a separate hail verse.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash discusses two readings of 24:43: mountains of hail sent down, or mountains of hail existing in the sky."}]}

{"id": "5:27/q04", "question": "Who are “the two sons of Adam”?", "turns_on": "Whether “Adam” names humanity's first father or a generic human/Israelite, and the crow's burial lesson and 5:32.", "positions": [{"id": "5:27/q04/p1", "position": "They are Adam's biological sons, Hābīl and Qābīl (Abel and Cain).", "reasons": "This is the majority view in al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Ālūsī. Name spellings vary (Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī). Al-Ṭabarī says a remote Israelite story would add little; al-Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Kuranyolu cite 5:31's first burial; Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān also cite the first-murderer report. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says an alternate Adam needs a clue; Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes generic singular “son of Adam” from this dual. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī questions Torah names due to textual transmission."}, {"id": "5:27/q04/p2", "position": "They were two Israelites, called Adam's sons as human descendants, or sons of another Israelite Adam.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk are cited; sacrifices and the law in 5:32 are offered as evidence, as is the Israelite request for a fire-consumed offering in 3:183. Al-Rāzī says it exposes ancient Jewish envy. Ṭabāṭabāʾī records the alternative Israelite Adam."}, {"id": "5:27/q04/p3", "position": "Their names are less important than the real moral event.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the general wording avoids legend, and the story's use remains even if treated hypothetically; he also reports some call it mythical, while Ömer Faruk Harman argues ancient parallels can preserve a historical event."}, {"id": "5:27/q04/p4", "position": "In an inward reading, they are the intellect and estimative faculty in Adam's heart.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī identifies Hābīl with intellect and Qābīl with estimation, each with a twin faculty; imagination serves estimation, practical reason serves intellect."}]}
{"id": "5:27/q05", "question": "What birth and sibling background do the reports give for the two sons?", "turns_on": "Reports vary on birth order, where conception occurred, and whether sibling marriage was lawful.", "positions": [{"id": "5:27/q05/p1", "position": "Eve bore boy-girl twins; Cain and his sister were born before Abel and his sister.", "reasons": "Names vary: Iqlīmā/Aqlima for Cain's twin and Labūdā/Luwaiza/Liuda for Abel's. Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī report twenty twin births and forty children except Seth, born alone. Ibn ʿAbbās says Adam saw forty thousand descendants. Some place Cain's birth one hundred years after descent; Ibn Isḥāq says Cain was conceived in Paradise before sin, Abel on earth after descent. Al-Kalbī says births were two years apart."}, {"id": "5:27/q05/p2", "position": "Adam's descendants became many and corrupt in his lifetime.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says he saw forty thousand descendants and witnessed adultery, drinking and corruption; al-Qurṭubī rejects an uncorroborated report of his daughter's fornication, questioning with whom it occurred."}, {"id": "5:27/q05/p3", "position": "A report gives Eve a daughter before Cain and Abel, then a jinn and a heavenly spouse for the brothers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣādiq calls the first daughter Luwaiza; al-Qurṭubī's version calls the first transgressing daughter ʿAnāq, killed before the brothers were born. This account denies that Adam married a daughter to a son."}, {"id": "5:27/q05/p4", "position": "Cain and his sister were born after Abel and his sister.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī records this alternate birth order without further evidence."}]}
{"id": "5:27/q06", "question": "How were the brothers to marry, and why did they dispute it?", "turns_on": "Whether exceptional cross-sibling marriage was allowed or the brothers received nonhuman spouses.", "positions": [{"id": "5:27/q06/p1", "position": "Adam directed each brother to marry the other's twin; Cain wanted his own more beautiful twin.", "reasons": "The only available women were sisters, so cross-birth marriages were temporarily allowed, not one's own twin; Ibn Jurayj says this lasted four generations. Al-Ṣādiq reasons Adam's religion matched Muhammad's, which forbade sibling marriage. Al-Qurṭubī doubts this account and prefers the cross-birth report."}]}

{"id": "5:27/q36", "question": "Why does this account follow the preceding discussion of Israel and its covenants?", "turns_on": "Sources offer several complementary links through envy, violence, ancestry, revealed knowledge and contrasting conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "5:27/q36/p1", "position": "It rebukes Jewish envy, violence and broken covenants while consoling and vindicating Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says the Jews plotted against the Prophet; Jishumī's al-Aṣamm and ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā warn that injustice returns on perpetrators.
